metadata.title: Persisting Progress Across Context Windows.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: how does a coding agent working a long feature list pick up correctly in a brand-new session? Lands the carry-out that a context window is a workspace, not memory — progress persists in a file and a git ledger, not in the agent.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> BCRY (file-across-the-boundary visual planted at B03, referenced in BCRY's carry-out line, not replayed as a second full composition)

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes an agent picking up mid-project must remember where it stopped — like memory carries over. It doesn't. It rereads a file that tracks progress. Here's how that actually works.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Claude just remembers where it left off? How does it resume?', hesitates on 'remembers', corrects to 'rereads'

props.text:

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('remembers' -> 'rereads') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: A context window has a limit. When an agent's conversation fills it, the session ends. The next session opens blank — no memory of what was done, what passed, what failed. Rereading everything burns half the new context. Guessing risks getting it wrong.

shot.new_visual_element: A session timeline: session one fills to the brim and stops, a boundary line, session two opens as an empty bar

production_viz.label: The session boundary is a wipe
production_viz.mechanic: A horizontal bar labelled 'Session 1' fills left to right on cream, capped 'context full'. A crimson vertical boundary line, 'session boundary'. A second bar, 'Session 2', starts completely empty beside it. A small footer reads 'No memory carries across.'

beats.narration_text: The fix: two external files. feature underscore list dot json is the source of truth — two hundred entries, each with an id and a status, incomplete or passing. Git is the ledger — one commit per finished feature, so the history can't be disputed. Each session reads the file, finds the first incomplete entry, implements it, tests it, commits, and marks it passing.

shot.new_visual_element: feature_list.json and a git log drawn side by side; a cycle arrow through read -> implement -> test -> commit -> mark passing

production_viz.label: Two files hold the truth
production_viz.mechanic: Two file cards side by side: 'feature_list.json' (entries with id + status) on the left, a git commit log on the right. Below, a five-step cycle arranged in a loop: Read -> Implement -> Test -> Commit -> Mark passing, the loop closing back to Read.

beats.act: 4 ANCHOR — the file across the boundary
beats.narration_text: Watch the file itself, across the boundary. Session one flips features one through fifty from incomplete to passing, one commit at a time. The boundary passes. Session two opens the same file, finds item fifty-one as the first incomplete entry, and starts there — no replay of the first fifty.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR: a vertical list of two hundred rows flipping status badges; a session-boundary divider; session two's read head lands on row 51

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — the file across the boundary
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A vertical list of numbered rows (feature ids) with status badges. Rows 1-50 flip from 'incomplete' to a crimson 'passing' check one by one during 'Session 1'. A dashed boundary line labelled 'session boundary'. In 'Session 2' a read-head marker drops onto row 51, the first still marked incomplete, and starts flipping rows from there.

beats.narration_text: This covers the checkpoint-and-resume mechanism only: the file, the git ledger, the boundary, and the first-incomplete lookup. It doesn't cover how the two-hundred-item list gets written in the first place — that's a separate step — or what exactly makes a feature count as passing.

shot.new_visual_element: The same anchor list, boxed with a solid line; two dashed unlabelled items outside the box for what's out of scope

production_viz.label: Exactly this far, and no further
production_viz.mechanic: A miniature version of B03's row list sits inside a solid-outlined box captioned 'the checkpoint mechanism'. Outside the box, across a dashed boundary, two faint unlabelled cards sit in a grey field: 'how the list is written' and 'what counts as passing' — no verdict, just what the mechanism doesn't cover.

beats.narration_text: A context window is a workspace, not memory — when it fills, the session ends, and what carries over is whatever got written to a file and a git commit, not anything the agent remembers.

props.quote: A context window is a workspace, not memory — when it fills, the session ends, and what carries over is whatever got written to a file and a git commit, not anything the agent remembers.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Ask Claude: externalize my agent's progress to a checkpoint file plus git commits, so a brand-new session can resume exactly where the last one stopped — then prove it by starting a fresh session and watching it pick up correctly. Liam, in for Bear.
